questions.q: What two elements combine to form a Pareto chart?
options: A bar chart sorted largest to smallest, plus a dual-axis line showing the cumulative percentage of total
A pie chart and a scatter plot layered together
Two identical bar charts placed side by side
A map with sales bars radiating from each region
questions.explain: A Pareto chart sorts individual values descending as bars, then overlays a cumulative percent-of-total line on a dual axis — exactly the technique Tableau's own documentation walks through.

questions.q: Does Tableau have a dedicated 'Waterfall' chart type in Show Me?
options: No — a waterfall is built using Gantt bars, with a running total determining each segment's starting position
Yes — it's a one-click option in Show Me
Yes, but only available in Tableau Public
No — waterfall charts cannot be built in Tableau at all
questions.explain: Tableau has no native Waterfall chart type. It's a real, working technique: Gantt bars sized by the measure (negative for decreases), positioned using a running-total table calculation.

questions.q: How is a funnel chart approximated in Tableau, given that it has no native Funnel chart type?
options: With a bar chart whose bars are centered and shrink in width stage over stage, using a calculated padding measure
With a native Funnel option available only in Tableau Server
With a scatter plot where point size represents the funnel stage
Funnel charts are impossible to approximate in Tableau
questions.explain: A funnel is approximated with centered bars that taper in width, achieved by adding a calculated padding measure (based on the gap between the current stage and the maximum stage value).

questions.q: In the waterfall chart technique, what determines each Gantt bar's starting position?
options: A running total (RUNNING_SUM) of the measure, minus the current segment's own value
The alphabetical order of the dimension labels
A fixed LOD expression scoped to the whole table
The bar's color property
questions.explain: The Gantt bar's start position is the running total of the measure up to that point, minus the current segment's own value — positioning each segment where the previous one left off.

questions.q: Why does this lesson show a real Tableau Help screenshot for the Pareto chart but an original diagram for waterfall and funnel charts?
options: Because Tableau documents the Pareto chart directly as an end-to-end build, while waterfall and funnel are real techniques with no dedicated official screenshot to source honestly
Because waterfall and funnel charts don't actually work in Tableau
Because Pareto charts are the only chart type covered in this lesson
Because the course policy forbids screenshots for any chart type
questions.explain: Tableau's help site has a dedicated, documented Pareto chart build with real screenshots. Waterfall and funnel charts are genuine working techniques, but since Tableau doesn't ship them as distinct chart types, there's no matching official screenshot — so the lesson shows the real mechanism as an original diagram instead of fabricating one.
